sceneEngine.textAlignmentWordAndBrightnessChanges: 2026-10-15: A text layer reads horizontalalign and verticalalign as Wallpaper Engine's enumerations and multiplies its colour by brightness only in the HDR pipeline, for interoperability; no code copied. Wallpaper Engine registers horizontalalign (left, center, right) and verticalalign (bottom, center, top; the registry is built in the order center, top, bottom) with the constructor default center for both (FUN_140256ae0, the 0x01010101 stored at +0x59c; the registrations at wallpaper64.c:422440-422650, which hold horizontalalign, verticalalign and anchor and no alignment), matching the whole word exactly, so case counts, and a key that is there with any other string or with a value that is not a string takes the registry's first entry (FUN_14025b450 for the horizontal one, FUN_14025b7c0 for the vertical one, whose first entry is center); read from the 2.8.42 binary. Before, TextLayer.cpp tested the words with ContainsSubstring (leftt, middle and any word that contained one matched), a text object's legacy alignment key stood in for a missing horizontalalign, the vertical placement fell back to the anchor string, and a key that was not a string left the field empty. Now ParseTextHorizontalAlign (any word but center and right is left) and ParseTextVerticalAlign (any word but top and bottom is center) decide every placement, WPTextObject defaults both keys to center and reads them as JSON (ReadMiscEnumWord: a key that is there and is no string is the registry's first entry; that an object such as a value wrapper takes the first entry too is inferred, since the loader that unwraps a wrapper before the enumeration reads it was not found, and no local scene has an object-valued alignment key), the alignment key is no longer read, createLayer({ text }) no longer forwards one, and TextLayerState::anchor, TextAnchorForObject and ReplaceAnchorAxis are gone: the node shift that places a text layer by its aligned edge, which stays until the placement change, is fed by TextAlignmentAnchor from the two words. A script's write of an alignment still has to be one of the words: the C-string setter the alignment registrations carry (FUN_14025a880, registered at wallpaper64.c:422478, with FUN_14025a960 mapping the stored entry back to its word) stores the registry's first entry for a word that matches none and ignores a null string, so if scripts write through it (not traced) 'middle' would give left (center vertically) and not be turned away; which path a script write takes is open, so the rejection stays. Brightness: the text object's colour functions (FUN_140257d70 into the composite target, FUN_140258050 direct) multiply the layer colour by brightness only when the context flag 0x2000 is set, the flag that also selects the 16-bit target format (wallpaper64.c:357046), which is scene.hdr here (general.hdr with general.bloom); ParseTextObj now gives g_Brightness the authored value only when scene.hdr and 1 otherwise, a property or script bound to the brightness is bound to the material only then (SceneRuntimeContext::BindMaterialBrightness with no materials keeps an unbound one alive, as it does for an image layer, so its script, which the context holds a pointer to, still runs). Image layers are not changed. Visible: none for the alignment words (all 802 local text objects carry valid words; probetext1 at 8 s is pixel-identical before and after); text with brightness other than 1 in a scene that is not HDR is drawn in its layer colour (233 local text layers carry one): 3413921910, whose three text layers have brightness 0 and every effect off, draws its white THURSDAY, date and clock where Wallpaper Engine does (THURSDAY x 1162 to 2292 in both, clock x 1611 to 1850 against 1612 to 1849) and drew nothing before. Not compared with a Wallpaper Engine frame: the HDR half of the brightness rule for text (the same flag's effect shows on an image layer of one local HDR scene, and the two local HDR scenes with text brightness do not settle it); two probe scenes, probetextb1 (not HDR) and probetextb2 (HDR with bloom), each with white-grey and orange text at brightness 0, 0.5, 1 and 2 on black, were queued for capture and the capture server was not running within 15 minutes, so they are uncaptured (this renderer draws every layer in its colour in the first and 0, 0.5, 1 and 2 times its colour, clipped, in the second). Cost: none (one comparison at parse). sceneEngine.textFontFaceChanges: 2026-10-15: A text layer's font faces are opened from their files once, picked by the name the system gives them, kept for the next layout, and a second face for a glyph the font lacks is looked for only when a layout meets such a glyph, for interoperability; no code copied. Wallpaper Engine loads the faces behind a glyph only when no loaded face has the code point and keeps the faces it loads by path (the glyph fallback FUN_1401ad670 and the face loader FUN_1401acaf0, which opens face 0 of a file; read from the 2.8.42 binary). Before, CreateFreeTypeFace read the whole file of the layer's font and CreateFallbackFace the whole file of its fallback (PingFang.ttc is 78,222,888 bytes, Arial Unicode 23.3 MB) on every MeasureFreeTypeText and RasterizeFreeTypeText, so three times per layout (the raster size measures once more), for every change of every text layer and whether or not the text had a glyph the font lacked; a collection's face was its index 0 (the Hong Kong cut of PingFang, the Black weight of Songti, the Bold weight of PT Mono). Now SystemFontResolver::ResolveSystemFont gives the path and the PostScript name (CoreText's kCTFontNameAttribute) of the matched face, and ResolveSystemFontPath is its path; TextLayerState::resolved_font_face carries the name from ResolveTextLayerFont (system and family fonts; cleared for a font the wallpaper ships) through TextLayer::SetFont, the script font setter and the cache identity. TextLayer.cpp's FaceCache holds at most 8 FT_Faces process-wide, keyed by file and index, the one unused longest dropped first, under g_freetype_mutex: FT_New_Face on the file (FreeType streams it; nothing is read into a buffer), the index being the one whose FT_Get_Postscript_Name matches (the file's other faces are probed once, a name the file lacks takes face 0 and is remembered as an alias), FT_Set_Char_Size for each use. A font the wallpaper ships stays a memory face over its VFS bytes and is not cached. FaceChain gives a layout its primary face and asks for the fallback face (PingFang SC, else Arial Unicode MS, else Helvetica, found by name) on the first missing glyph, once per layout; the glyph chain itself is unchanged. Visible: Latin text in Arial or Helvetica and the asset-font probes are pixel-identical (probetext1 and probetext2 at 8 s and 15 s, before and after); a font in a collection draws its regular face (Songti SC, PT Mono) and Han punctuation from the Simplified Chinese cut (the fullwidth and ideographic commas and the ideographic full stop move from 0.29 to 0.36 em above the baseline to within 0.03 em of it). Cost, measured: the 106 tests of text_object_runtime_test took 14.9 s before and its 114 tests 0.7 s after; the 20 layouts of ASystemFontIsOpenedOnceAndNotForEveryLayout (ten of a clock in a system font, ten of the same with a Han glyph) went from 120 font file reads and 700 ms to 2 opens and 3 ms. Up to 8 faces stay open (memory-mapped by FreeType, pages touched only); no per-frame work. Not checked: the lock-screen extension's sandbox with a face opened by path (the open is the one the byte read made, plus FreeType's mapping of the same file); a face whose file has changed in size or modification time, or is gone, since it was opened is dropped before a layout takes its faces, so the next use opens the file as it is (FreeType maps the file, and a font a user installed and then truncated in place under an open face would fault the read), and a face is looked at for the file's size and time once per layout, not per frame. sceneEngine.fogEffectCompositeChanges: 2026-10-15: Scene fog falls on an effect layer where the layer sits, for interoperability; no code copied. The layer's own pass and its effect chain are drawn into a card of their own, from an ortho camera and with no transform, where world position is card pixels while g_EyePosition is the scene camera's eye, so the fog compiled into that pass followed the distance from the card's centre: a layer under an effect carried a radial vignette, tone 0.99 at 56 px falling to 0.72 at 250 px on the moon of one local scene, where Wallpaper Engine dims the whole disc evenly. Wallpaper Engine's image-layer setup (FUN_140206ae0; a sibling setup, FUN_1401ebbc0, sets the same two combos without the removal below) builds the layer's composite from the passthrough material it names (effectpassthrough_4 when the device level is above 2, FUN_1401ecae0, effectpassthrough otherwise) with its BLENDMODE and FOG_COMPUTED=1 combos, then removes FOG and FOG_COMPUTED from them again unless the layer's own material has FOG on (a lookup of FOG in the material's combo table: absent or 0 removes them; the moon's material sets no combos and its shader, genericimage4, defaults FOG on, and Wallpaper Engine fogs it, so the table holds the shader's default too), so a layer whose material takes no fog gets none from the composite; that this composite is the pass drawn at the layer's model matrix is read from the frame below, not from the decompile. LoadMaterial gains WPShaderInfo::defer_fog / fog_deferred: a pass that defers leaves the fog out and reports that its FOG combo was on in a fogged scene. ParseImageObj defers the fog of the layer's first pass and of every effect pass and, when the first pass would have taken it, appends effectpassthrough_4 as the chain's last effect (MakeFogCompositeEffect), with a white g_Color4 as the colour-blend passthrough has because the layer's colour and alpha are already in what it copies; the chain's last pass is the final pass, so it is drawn with the layer's model matrix and the scene camera and the fog is measured where the layer sits. The pass is added whenever the layer's own material takes fog, whether or not the layer's own pass is drawn, so a layer an effect generates (copybackground off) is fogged, where only an effect pass of its own with a FOG combo fogged it before; that rests on the decompiled setup alone, which checks one bit of the object's flags and never the copybackground bit, and no frame of Wallpaper Engine's shows such a layer in a fogged scene (the one local fogged scene has none). A layer another layer samples draws its last pass into its composite from the layer-local camera too, so the sampled picture carries fog measured in the card, for a plain layer as for an effect layer and the same as before this change (drawn with and without it beside a card that shows the composite: the pixels read were identical). A layer whose material takes no fog, compose, fullscreen, puppet and colour-blend layers, text layers, and assets without effectpassthrough_4 keep what they drew. Established: the decompile above, and Wallpaper Engine's frame of the scene (the moon layer's mean luma by distance from the disc centre, ratio ours/WE 1.03-1.08 in the five inner rings and 0.96 and 0.89 in the two outer ones before, 0.996-1.001 in every ring after; no pixel outside the disc changes). Cost: one layer-sized pass per effect layer whose material takes fog in a fogged scene, none otherwise (on the moon scene, measured on the committed build against its base: 9 to 10 passes a frame and +1,064,960 bytes of render targets for the 512 x 512 layer; CPU per drawFrame not measurably changed, 16 interleaved runs of 600 frames per build giving a median of 0.35 ms for both, spread over 0.19-0.45 ms, where one pass of the frame takes about 0.02-0.04 ms to encode; one pair of runs of an earlier prototype of this change had read 0.21-0.23 ms and 0.28-0.31 ms, about 0.07 ms more; GPU time not isolated, as the energy runs of that prototype differed from one another by more than the prototype and its base differ). Tests: MetalSceneDraw.AnEffectLayerIsFoggedWhereItSitsAsAPlainLayerIsOnBothRenderers (distance and height fog; the layer under a copy effect equals the plain layer at the centre, sides and corners of its card, the two renderers equal), .AnEffectLayersColourAndAlphaAreAppliedOnceWhenItIsFoggedWhereItSitsOnBothRenderers (the same with the layer's colour and alpha, applied once), .AnEffectLayerWhoseEffectsAScriptSwitchesIsFoggedWhereItSitsOnBothRenderers (the effect off and on), .AnEffectLayerThatMakesItsOwnPictureIsFoggedWhereItSitsOnBothRenderers (copybackground off) and .AnEffectLayerWhoseMaterialTakesNoFogIsNotFoggedOnBothRenderers.
sceneEngine.comboFlagChanges: 2026-10-15: A flag bound to a string property by name alone follows the string as a flag, for interoperability; no code copied. The case that matters is a layer's or effect's `visible` bound to a combo. A scene that turned a toggle into a combo keeps `{"user": "clock1", "value": true}` on the layers the toggle showed. DynamicValue::update(const std::string&) set the flag to false for every string unless a condition was attached, and a binding copies the property's flag, so those layers were never visible, whatever the choice. It now sets the flag from StringIsTrue (`true` in any case, or `1`), the rule RuntimeScalarValue::String and asBool already had, now one function in ProjectProperties that compares in place and allocates nothing; the condition form still compares the choice with its condition, and a numeric setting bound to a choice still reads 0. A combo whose project.json value is a number stays a number, so a bare flag bound to it is on for any whole number but 0 while the combo keeps its authored value, where the choice the app sends is a string and `2` is off. The rule is the flag's, so it holds for every bool a setting binds by name to a string property (a layer's or effect's `visible`, a puppet animation layer's, the camera shake's and the load-only bloom and camera-parallax switches, a rope's `uvscrolling` and `uvsmoothing`, a text layer's outline, blur and shadow switches), whatever the property's kind (combo, text input, file, directory, texture), and for a string a script returns for a flag. Established: Wallpaper Engine's frames of a scene whose combo is at its default `1` draw the two black opacity-mask cover layers bound this way (the date shows black under the clock, and the clock's top and bottom edges fade; with the covers forced visible ours reproduced the reference rows 236/236, 248/248, 245/244, where the stem of the `1` was a flat 255 against the reference 250 falling to 129 at the baseline row). The decompiled `visible` setter (FUN_1401e1a90) takes a JSON boolean and registers the binding (FUN_1401a4db0), and nothing read shows how a string reaches it, so what Wallpaper Engine does with a choice other than `1` is not established and those follow the string rule above. Cost: the flag is computed on every string update, a scripted string's every tick included (FillDynamicValueFromJS), with a length check and at most four character compares, in place and with no allocation, where it set a constant. Tests: ChoiceProperty.ABindingWithoutAConditionReadsTheChoiceAsAFlag, .ABindingWithoutAConditionFollowsTheChoiceWhileTheSceneRuns, .AConnectedFlagIsTheChoicesTruthAndAConditionStillCompares, .AStringIsATrueFlagOnlyForTrueInAnyCaseOrOne, .AnEffectBoundToAChoiceWithoutAConditionIsBuiltForATrueChoice and .ANumberDeclaredAsTheChoiceIsAFlagByBeingNonZero in project_property_preview_test, and ScriptRuntimeCompat.AVisibleScriptThatReturnsAStringIsReadAsAFlag in script_runtime_compat_test.
sceneEngine.effectFinalDepthChanges: 2026-10-15: The last pass of an image layer's effects, the one that puts the layer into the scene, is drawn with the layer's own authored depth test and depth write, not the ones its effect pass authored, except that a layer Wallpaper Engine sorts in a scene that sorts takes no write. SceneImageEffectLayer gains SetFinalDepth (an optional SceneDepthState). ParseImageObj hands it, beside the blending it already hands SetFinalBlend, the depth_test of the layer's own material and its depth_write unless Scene::opaque_first (a perspective scene with transparentsorting) holds and ImageLayerIsSorted finds the layer's own material blending, read before the effect chain turns it to normal, translucent or additive; a material that is normal (which disabled and an unknown word also parse to) or alphatocoverage keeps the write. ResolveEffect copies both onto the final pass's material next to the blend, so ResolveSceneDepthState applies them on a depth-attached target in both renderers. A layer that never calls SetFinalDepth (a text layer drawn through effects) keeps its pass's own state. Before the change the pass kept the effect's authored state, usually depthtest and depthwrite disabled, so a translucent layer authored depthtest enabled was drawn over an opaque depth-written model with no occlusion. Established against Wallpaper Engine 2.8.42's binary and frames. Binary, the depth state (observed): FUN_1401ebf60, which draws one pass of an effect chain, saves the pass's blending, depthtest and depthwrite bytes (offsets 0x1f0, 0x1f2 and 0x1f3 of the pass: the blending, and the two 'disabled' flags that FUN_140155fc0 applies when a pass begins, FUN_140157430 undoes when it ends and FUN_140206ae0 writes back as the material's "depthtest" and "depthwrite") around a virtual (slot 0x108) of the layer object on the final pass, restoring them after it. The image object class (constructor FUN_1401fac50, vtable 0x1404911a8) implements that slot at 0x140209160: it writes the pass's blending byte as additive (2) when the layer's colour blend mode (object +0x32c) is 31 and as the blending byte of the layer's own material pass (object +0x498, the pass FUN_140208670 draws an effect-free image layer with and FUN_140206ae0 serialises) otherwise, and copies that material pass's 0x1f2 and 0x1f3 onto the pass; it writes nothing else, so culling stays the effect pass's. A composition or solid layer is an object of the same class, so the editor's composelayer_depthtest and solidlayer_depthtest models get the same copy (interoperability; no code copied). Binary, the sort (observed): a scene whose flags carry 0x1000 (transparentsorting) is drawn by FUN_14018aac0 in two sets: the objects that do not carry flag 0x100, in scene order, then the ones that do, in the order FUN_1401865c0 produces: a key per object, dot(the object's world position at +0x128..+0x130, a float3 of the render context), minus infinity for an object carrying flag 0x200, sorted by descending key with a stable sort (the insertion sort FUN_14019ee60 up to 32 objects, the buffered merge FUN_14019ef50 beyond; equal keys keep scene order). The object-creating function FUN_14018ff60 puts an object with flag 0x100 in the sorted list (this+0x170) and in the hash set (this+0x188) that the first loop of FUN_14018aac0 skips. The image object constructor FUN_1401fac50 sets flag 0x100 unless the blending byte (offset 0x1f0) of its material pass (the pass at object +0x498) is 0 or 3: the enum is normal 0, translucent 1, additive 2, alphatocoverage 3 (the name table at 0x1404e9390 behind the 'blending' property that FUN_1401577e0 registers at offset 0x1f0, the names FUN_1401531c0 returns, and the ADDITIVE and ALPHATOCOVERAGE combos that FUN_140154480 defines for 2 and 3), so a repository BlendMode::Normal or Disable is the unmarked 0 and AlphaToCoverage the unmarked 3. It would also set it for a passthrough layer (flag 0x20) whose flag 0x40 is clear whatever its blending, but flag 0x40 is copybackground (setter FUN_1401ef350) and is applied by the load step (the load virtual through FUN_1401e6f50) only after the constructor FUN_1401fac50 has made the sort decision, and the base constructor FUN_1401e6980 starts the flags at 0x8040, so that decision always sees 0x40 set and passthrough changes nothing. So a translucent or additive image layer is drawn after the unmarked ones, back to front, and its write hides nothing that comes after it, while a normal or alphatocoverage layer is drawn in scene order in the first set with its write, which hides the farther sorted layers drawn after it. That the float3 is the view direction is inferred from the frames. Some other object kinds (the constructor FUN_140256ae0 and two inline constructors in FUN_14018ff60) set flag 0x100 unconditionally; those kinds were not read. Frames, the depth test: a scene whose star glare layers (translucent, depthtest and depthwrite enabled, an effect pass authoring depthtest disabled) sit at the stars' centres shows each star as a white sphere with a warm glow only outside the silhouette in Wallpaper Engine (disc core 248,244,230, std 13) and as a smooth warm disc (254,234,206, std 6) without the test, and with the glare tint black the disc fell to 0.41-0.44 of its brightness, i.e. the sprite was composited over it; with the test the same scene's star discs are white with a warm glow outside, as Wallpaper Engine's. Frames, the depth write: with the write kept for the glare cards, the card of the nearest star (a layer authored translucent, depthtest and depthwrite enabled, with an effect pass authoring neither) writes depth over its whole quad, transparent texels included, and this engine draws the layers that are not in its opaque set in scene order, so every farther layer drawn after it fails the depth test inside the card: the other stars' glows, the nebula layers (a dark rectangle with hard edges around a star) and the hover HUD of a farther star (ring, leader line and underline; its text label sets no depth state and stays). Wallpaper Engine's frame of 3509243656 shows a farther body's hover ring, leader line and underline whole across the glare card of a nearer star, and no star's glow cut by another star's card. A seeded A/B (the script engine's Math.random seeded so two builds run the same simulation, 12 s in, pointer fed at the centre) over seeds 1 to 3, 5 to 8, 10, 13 and 14 differs by 13 to 86 thousand of 7 million pixels per frame; with the test and no write the rectangle and the glows are gone, in seed 14 a star's ring and leader line are back, and the star discs stay white. A ring of the star's own HUD, in the glare card's plane, is drawn with the write (equal depth passes), while a farther layer under a nearer star's card is not, so the failure is a farther layer under a nearer card, not a coplanar one. Survey of the 100 local scenes: 14 image layers with effects author a depth-tested material (3509243656: seven star layers; 3477054430: a moon layer; 3589454154 and 3665954520: three solid layers each), and only 3509243656 was compared with a Wallpaper Engine frame. Two are perspective scenes that sort (3509243656 and 3589454154); the effect layers of 3509243656 that author a depth write are all translucent and 3589454154 has none, so no local frame shows a layer that keeps its write in a sorting scene and that half rests on the binary and the test. 3665954520 (2D, no depth attachment) is byte for byte unchanged; 3477054430 (a moon layer, no sorting) draws identical pixels with and without the write, and the test draws about 500 of 7 million pixels at 3456x2024 of star sprites over the moon that Wallpaper Engine's frame does not have (38 to 44 levels off on average, against 2 to 3 without the test), a likely star-shell-nearer-than-the-moon question left open; 3589454154 (Saturn) differs by no more than 13 pixels, about as many as two runs of one build do, between no depth state, the test alone and the test with the write, outside its clock text. Not done: the text object's slot-0x108 virtual (vtable 0x140491950, at 0x140258580) writes its final pass's blending as translucent and its depth-test flag from the object's own state (depth test on unless bit 0x400 of the render context's flags or the byte at text object +0x5a0 is set, the condition that also selects the depth-tested font materials) and leaves the depth-write flag alone; a text layer drawn through effects still keeps its pass's own state here. The back-to-front sort itself is not done (the compiled graph's pass order is fixed while scripts move layers every frame, so it needs its own design and a measurement), so a plain translucent layer authored depthwrite still hides farther layers drawn after it in a sorting scene, and this engine's opaque set (nodes without effects, normal or disabled blending, depth-tested) is narrower than Wallpaper Engine's unmarked set, which also holds effect layers and layers without a depth test. Cost: none per frame, no new pass or target (a sorted layer's final pass has one depth write fewer); a compose or solid layer authored depth-tested with effects now tests its result against a depth-attached scene, as the binary's copy does. Tests: MetalSceneDraw.ALayerDrawnThroughEffectsKeepsItsOwnDepthTestAndWriteOnBothRenderers draws seventeen authored cases through both renderers. Nine go through an orthographic canvas: an image layer with and without a pass-through effect, authoring test and write, test only, neither, and neither under an effect pass that authors both; a solid layer and a composition layer authoring a test only; a composition layer authoring neither under an effect pass that authors both. Without the change the effect cases whose layer authors depth draw the layer over the nearer card and the cases whose layer authors neither under an effect pass that authors both hide it, on both renderers. Eight go through a perspective camera with transparentsorting and a farther translucent card: a translucent layer, an additive layer, a solid layer, a composition layer, and a translucent layer whose farther card runs the same effect, each testing and writing, are hidden over the nearer card and cut nothing out of the farther card, over which they are transparent as a glare card is (the five read nothing there if the write is kept, on both renderers); a layer authoring neither is the geometry reference; a normal layer and an alphatocoverage layer that test and write keep their write and hide the farther card (both draw the farther card over the layer, on both renderers, if the write is dropped from every layer of a sorting scene).
sceneEngine.wrapLoopTimelines: 2026-10-15: A timeline that sets wraploop now closes every curve on the first key's value at the timeline's length, as Wallpaper Engine does; before, a looping curve whose last key differed from its first held that key to the end of the length and then jumped back to the start, a hard cut once per lap (measured on the local scenes: every loop-mode scale and colour timeline sets wraploop and 7 of the 11 have a last key that differs from the first; for instance one four-layer colour timeline held roughly (0.33, 0.33, 0.56) for the last quarter of its lap and then jumped to roughly (0.96, 0.96, 0.87)). ResolveScalarAnimation (the one curve reader behind origin, alpha, scale, angles, colour, light intensity and shader constants) calls CloseCurveAtLoopLength after sorting the keys. Established against Wallpaper Engine 2.8.42's decompile: FUN_1401a96b0 reads wraploop and sets bit 0x10 of the timeline's state beside length, fps, mode, random and startpaused; the sites that read a timeline's curves into keyframes (the generic setting reader FUN_1401a4db0, FUN_1401f1bc0 for the three curves of a vec3 setting, and the object reader that handles the two further scalar curves) then run FUN_1401a98b0(length, curve) on each curve when the bit is set. That function pops keys while the length is below the last key's frame and at least two keys remain, then either sets the last key's value to the first key's (when the last key is on the length) or appends a key at the length holding the first key's value, and copies the first key's front handle, negated, to the closing key's back handle (clearing its back-handle flag when the first key has no front handle). The mirror mode is still not implemented. Cost: load time only; the curves have at most one key more and nothing is added per frame. Tests: ScriptRuntimeCompat.WrapLoopClosesACurveOnItsFirstKeyAtTheTimelinesLength, .WrapLoopSeamMirrorsTheFirstKeysHandle; SceneSchema.WrapLoopTimelinesReturnToTheirFirstKeyOnEveryAnimatedSetting (the last fails on the previous source: the scale holds its last key); no wallpaper-specific rules.
sceneEngine.nodeTimelineChanges: 2026-10-15: A layer's scale and angles, and an image layer's colour, play their authored timelines the way origin and alpha already did; before, a pure animation object ({value, animation:{c0..c2, options, relative}}) kept the scene file's value, so a start-paused or running timeline showed its rest value (4 local scenes key scale, 3 key angles, 1 keys colour). RegisterNodeOriginSetting is replaced by RegisterNodeTransformSettings, which binds a layer's origin, scale and angles together: a script or user property as before, else the authored timeline on a NodeVec3Animation (the former NodeOriginAnimation: three curves on one playback, relative keys offset the authored value, unkeyed axes keep it), else no binding. SceneRuntimeContext::RegisterNodeScale and RegisterNodeRotation take the animation, apply its first frame at registration and sample it in their tick loops like the translate loop (a frame that has not moved is not sampled again). The six registration sites (group placeholders, text, image, particle, model/camera/misc objects, lights) call the one helper, and the parse-time dynamic_scale/dynamic_angles flags it replaces are removed. Settings the editor keyed together (options.parent.key, followed through any chain among origin, scale and angles; an unknown parent or a cycle leaves a setting its own clock) share the first one's playback, so a start-paused parent holds the angles and scale keyed under it. An image layer's colour timeline (ResolveVec3Animation, a clock of its own) builds the layer with its first colour and drives every material that takes g_Color4, the layer's and each effect pass as the user-bound colour does, through RegisterMaterialColorAnimation, keeping the alpha. A script or user property on the setting still wins and registers no clock (the precedence of the colour sources is: script or user property, else timeline), and the HDR brightness tint multiplies the timeline's colour like the others because the timeline writes through ApplyMaterialColor; a static setting allocates nothing. Established against Wallpaper Engine 2.8.42's decompile: one generic setting reader (FUN_1401a4db0, which also reads `script` and `scriptproperties`; nothing in it depends on which property the setting is) reads `animation`, keeps `options.parent.key` and `options.name`, and applies `relative` to the c0..c2 curves with the setting's own `value` components; FUN_1401a96b0 reads length, fps, mode, random, startpaused and wraploop into one state that FUN_1401a8c10 fills (mirror, single and start-paused are flags beside the curves, not a different evaluator), so the origin rules hold for scale, angles and colour. That linked settings share one clock follows the editor's parent/children keys and the camera-shot and shader-constant groups already here; no frame of Wallpaper Engine shows a paused scale or angles timeline (3819684521's 'Media Area' start-paused scale timeline is not played by this change either: that setting also carries an event-only script, a setting with a `script` key counts as script-bound and its timeline is dropped, and playing it needs a getAnimation scoped to the property first, because the script's no-name getAnimation() resolves the unnamed alpha clock; the scene is unaffected). The mirror mode (flag 1) is not implemented, here or for origin and alpha; wraploop is (see wrapLoopTimelines). Cost: one three-curve evaluation per animated node per tick, skipped while the playhead has not moved, and one per animated colour; nothing when no timeline is authored. Tests: SceneSchema.ScaleAndAnglesTimelinesPlayLikeOriginTimelines, .ScaleAndAnglesTimelinesStartingPausedHoldTheirFirstPoseUntilPlayed, .ScaleTimelineLoopsOnOneClockAndKeepsUnkeyedAxes, .LinkedOriginScaleAndAnglesTimelinesShareTheirParentsClock, .ScaleAndAnglesTimelinesDoNotOverrideAScriptOrUserProperty, .ScaleTimelineKeepsAnAnchoredLayersEdgeOnItsScaledSize, .ScaleTimelineScalesAParentsChildren, .ScaleAndAnglesTimelinesPlayOnTextParticleLightAndModelObjects (the text, particle, light and model registration sites and a text parent with children), .ImageColourTimelineTintsEveryLayerMaterialAsItPlays, .ImageColourSourcesKeepTheirPrecedenceAndTheHdrBrightnessMultipliesEach; MetalSceneDraw.AnAnimatedScaleAndAnglesTimelineMoveALayerOnBothRenderers, .AnAnimatedLayerColourTintsTheLayerOnBothRenderers (both fail on the previous source, on Compatibility and on Native Metal); no wallpaper-specific rules.
sceneEngine.layerTransformMatrixChanges: 2026-10-15: A scene script can ask a layer where it stands, `layer.getTransformMatrix()`, for interoperability; no code copied. Wallpaper Engine registers `getTransformMatrix` on the layer binding it builds for every layer (the registration FUN_1401e0530, which also registers `origin`, `scale`, `angles`, `getParent` and `getChildren`); its handler FUN_1401df5e0 calls the layer's virtual at vtable +0x80 and copies the 16 floats (64 bytes) it returns into the script's matrix. That slot is the layer's world matrix: the base class's FUN_1401850a0 builds it from the layer's translate, scale and angles, applies the parent's attachment transform (the parent's virtual at +0x78) when the layer hangs from an attachment, and multiplies the parent's own matrix in, with no exception for a fullscreen layer; the image and text classes override the slot (FUN_1401fd3f0, FUN_140256e10) to move its translation by an offset of their own along the matrix's own axes; an image layer's is its anchor offset (half its size toward the centre, from its `alignment`, written by the size setter FUN_1402066a0, zero for the centre), so for an anchored image layer the translation is the centre of its quad and not the anchor. The cursor hit test FUN_14019dbb0 reads the same slot and builds the quad as that translation less half the size along each axis, and adds the camera parallax offset to the translation only afterwards, so the parallax is not in the matrix; the hit test's further hook at +0xa8 does nothing for an image layer (the stub `xor al, al; ret`) and shifts a text layer (FUN_1402585c0, an offset chosen by a nine-way setting from the text's bounds), which the matrix a script reads does not include. The frame was read from the scripts of the user's own local wallpapers, which compare `getTransformMatrix().m[12]` with `engine.canvasSize.x / 2` and `m[13]` with `engine.canvasSize.y / 2` to tell which half of the screen a widget that sits inside a group is on: the matrix is the layer's world transform in canvas units, y up, column after column as a script's Mat4 keeps it. Before, the wrapper `__createLayer` builds had no such method, so a script that called it threw `not a function`; in `init()` that skipped the rest of it. The Media Info widget of a local scene calls it in the init of its clock and text container scripts, so the defaults those scripts store in `shared` were never set (invisible with the widget group off, which is its default, because nothing reads them then). SceneRuntimeContext::NodeTransformMatrix brings the node's matrix up to date (UpdateTrans) and returns ModelTrans, the matrix the node is placed with in the graph: its translate, scale and turn with every ancestor's, an attachment's bone transform included, and for a fullscreen layer its own placement (it ignores its parents, as it is drawn); a name with no node answers the identity. It is not the matrix the layer is drawn with: a layer drawn through its effects renders from an identity of its own (the render-transform override), and a camera parallax offsets only the copy the shader reads. The native `__layerGetTransformMatrix` hands the 16 numbers to the wrapper, which builds a Mat4 through a frozen `__WEMat4` name (beside `__WEVec2/3/4`) so a script that reassigns the global `Mat4` cannot change what the host returns. Cost: a call brings one node chain up to date (nothing when it is clean) and allocates 16 numbers and a Mat4; nothing runs unless a script calls it. Not done: `getChildren`, `setParent`, `rotateObjectSpace`, `lookAt`, `lookAtYaw` and `getAttachment*`, registered beside it, still throw `not a function` (listed under Known limitations); an image layer with an `alignment` other than the centre answers the centre of its quad here as it does there (the node's translate is the anchor plus the offset the runtime derives, and `layer.origin` reads the anchor); left unestablished: a text layer's offset (the override above and the hook at +0xa8) was not compared with this renderer's text anchor, and since Wallpaper Engine's getter has no fullscreen exception a fullscreen layer inside a transformed group answers its parents' product there and its own placement here. Checked: the Media Info widget's scene run headless through offscreen_scene_probe with the widget group on, with and without playback events: the script errors it logged (168 in three frames, 43 of them `not a function`) are gone and no other error appears; without playback events the picture differs only in the clock's own time, and with a playing event the widget's parts its scripts now place differ (the clock text that stayed visible beside the cover is gone), for which no Wallpaper Engine frame exists, so that picture is not compared. Tests: ScriptRuntimeCompat.LayerTransformMatrixPlacesAChildWhereItsParentsPutIt (a group at (100, 200) scaled by two puts a child at (10, 20) at (120, 240), read by a third layer's init through `shared`), .LayerTransformMatrixCarriesTheTurnAndScaleOfItsParents (a quarter turn: position (60, 220), axes turned and doubled, a point transformed, a fullscreen-style layer that ignores its parent, a layer with a render-transform override, a copy per call, a reassigned global Mat4), .LayerTransformMatrixFollowsALayerWhereverItMoves (the left or right half of the canvas as the parent moves, and right after a script's own writes) and .LayerTransformMatrixOfALayerWithoutANodeIsTheIdentity, and, with layers the parser built, SceneSchema.LayerTransformMatrixOfParsedLayersIsWhereTheirParentsPutThem (a group at (100, 200) scaled by two puts a child at (10, 20) at (120, 240) and a child drawn through a copy effect at (30, 0) at (160, 200); answering the render transform instead fails it) and SceneSchema.LayerTransformMatrixOfAnAnchoredLayerIsTheCentreOfItsQuad (an image anchored left answers half its drawn width right of the anchor `layer.origin` reads, and follows a script that moves the anchor); all six failed with `TypeError: not a function` before the change.
sceneEngine.canvasPerspectiveCameraChanges: 2026-10-15: The camera that a 2D scene's perspective layers (particles and models with the `perspective` flag) draw through is seated where Wallpaper Engine seats it, for interoperability; no code copied. It sat 1000 units in front of the canvas with a field of view derived to show the canvas from there (42 degrees for a canvas 768 high, 94 for 2160), an assumption written out in ParseCamera, Scene::FrameCanvas, SceneRuntimeContext::ApplySceneZoom and ApplyCameraFillMode. Both cameras map the canvas plane identically and disagree about everything off it: a particle 500 units out was twice its size and one past 1000 units was behind the eye and not drawn, where Wallpaper Engine's eye is (visible height / 2) / tan(fov / 2) away with fov the scene's perspectiveoverridefov, so a flake never grows past D / (D - z) for the scene's own D. A new FitCanvasPerspective (SceneCamera.h/.cpp) seats the camera: the field of view is left alone, the eye's depth is CalculatePersperctiveDistance(fov, the canvas camera's visible height), the near plane is 5 and the far plane max(D + 1000, 15000); ParseCamera, Scene::FrameCanvas (a camera layer), SceneRuntimeContext::ApplySceneZoom (the scene zoom) and ApplyCameraFillMode (fill modes) call it, and a camera whose field of view is locked, a perspective scene's, is left alone. The field of view of a 2D scene's camera is general.perspectiveoverridefov, 95 when it is absent or not positive, held to 0.1..179.9; general.fov no longer reaches it. perspectiveoverridefov is read from a file of any package version (WPSceneGeneral::FromJson took it from version 21 on only), and, now that every version carries it, it no longer sets the field of view of a scene with a perspective projection either: ResolvePerspectiveFov took it before general.fov, and FUN_1401891a0 reads fov (+0x140) when the scene's orthographic bit is clear; no local perspective scene carries the key. CalculatePersperctiveFov has no caller left and is removed. The eye the shaders of these layers read as g_EyePosition is not the camera's position: the parser bakes (canvas centre, 2000) for a particle, as FUN_1401891a0 stores 2000.0 (0x44fa0000) as the z of an orthographic scene's eye whatever the field of view, but WPShaderValueUpdater::UpdateUniforms overwrote that with the perspective camera's position, which was 1000 units out and would now be D (from about 350 to 12400 units across the local scenes). The particle trail shaders (common_particles.h ComputeParticleTrailTangents) and the rope trail geometry shader (orientation 0) orient their ribbons by the vector from the particle to that eye, and genericparticle, genericropeparticle and the generic model shaders read it for their view direction, so the update now keeps the eye over the view's centre at kCanvasShaderEyeDepth (2000, SceneCamera.h, which the parser's baked value uses too) for a camera whose field of view is not locked, and only a perspective scene's camera supplies its own position. A trail scene's ribbons therefore come from an eye at 2000 where they came from one at 1000; no Wallpaper Engine frame of a trail scene was compared, and the claim rests on the decompiled constant and the parser's existing baked value. Established: the decompiled view setup (FUN_1401e5b60 and its twin FUN_140184f00 set the view's depth translation to -(1 / (tan(fov / 2) / (1 / projection[1][1]))), that is -(H / 2) / tan(fov / 2) from the orthographic projection's y scale, for an object with the perspective bit); the projection set up for it (near 5.0, far max(that distance + 1000, 15000), the context's field of view); FUN_1401891a0 (the effective field of view is the scene's perspectiveoverridefov when the scene's orthographic bit is set and its fov otherwise, clamped to 0.1..179.9, with the camera eye of an orthographic scene at the canvas centre 2000 units out) and the scene constructor FUN_140186c90 (defaults 50 and 95); the scene's property table registers perspectiveoverridefov with no version condition. Observed: the earlier comparison of Wallpaper Engine's own frames showed 2.7 times as many visible dots in a snow wallpaper as Wallpaper Engine's (63 and 60 against 20 and 25), giant flakes missing in another and flakes past 1000 units missing in a third. A headless render of a local wallpaper with 7 perspective particle systems, perspectiveoverridefov 35.22 on a 2160 canvas (distance 3400 units against 1000), drew long radial streaks before and only small flecks after, as its Wallpaper Engine screenshot has; one with the default 95 and particles that stay on the canvas plane came out identical. No orthographic scene in the local comparison set uses a 3D model, so none was compared. A re-render of the snow wallpaper 2524161239 (a staged copy of the Workshop item, 1728x1012, 8 s, seed 1) during review counted 73 flakes seen only through the old camera against 28 seen only through the new one, 2.6 times fewer, in line with the 60 and 63 against 20 and 25 of the earlier comparison; the other two wallpapers were not re-measured. Cost: none; no pass, draw or per-frame work is added, and the camera's matrices are recomputed only when the canvas is reframed. Tests: SceneSchema.A2DScenesPerspectiveCameraSitsWhereItsFieldOfViewPutsTheEye (field of view, eye depth, near and far, the canvas plane mapped as the orthographic view maps it, magnification D / (D - z) and visibility past 1000 units), .TheFieldOfViewOfA2DScenesPerspectiveCameraIsReadFromAnyPackageVersion and .CameraZoomTimelineRevealsFullCanvasWithoutResizingRenderTargets (changed from the old rule: the zoom now moves the eye and keeps the field of view) in scene_schema_tests; CameraFraming.APerspectiveCameraKeepsItsLensAndFollowsEveryWayTheCanvasIsFramed (every fill mode and FrameCanvas) in layer_texture_reference_test; MetalSceneDraw.APerspectiveLayerIsSeenFromTheEyeDistanceOfTheScenesFieldOfViewOnBothRenderers (card width at 500, 1100 and 1400 units out on both renderers); Renderers.APerspectiveParticleReadsTheEyeTwoThousandUnitsOutWhateverTheLens in particle_parity_test and SceneSchema.A2DScenesPerspectiveModelReadsTheEyeTwoThousandUnitsOutWhateverTheLens (g_EyePosition of a perspective particle and model at 2000 over the view's centre for fields of view of 30, 40, 95 and 150 degrees and after a reframe); SceneSchema.PerspectiveShotsInheritSceneFovUnlessExplicitlyOverridden (changed: a perspective scene keeps fov whatever perspectiveoverridefov says). Each of the new tests fails with its part of the change removed.
sceneEngine.cursorWorldPositionChanges: 2026-10-15: A perspective scene's scripts read the point where the cursor ray reaches the camera's far plane as `input.cursorWorldPosition`, for interoperability; no code copied. Wallpaper Engine's host function for it is FUN_14018e070(this, float* out, bool screen): the SceneScript DLL's `input` getters (scenescript64.dll, the callbacks registered next to the `cursorWorldPosition`, `cursorScreenPosition` and `cursorLeftDown` names) call a host slot with the flag 0 for `cursorWorldPosition` and 1 for `cursorScreenPosition`, and this is the one function of that shape found in the executable. With the flag clear it calls FUN_14019df90, a glm::unProject, with the window point (pointer x, 1 - pointer y, 0.5), the viewport (0, 0, 1, 1), the scene's view matrix (the lookAt FUN_14019d920 writes through scene + 0x38 each frame, with the camera shake already in the eye) and its projection (scene + 0x40): the inverse of projection * view applied to (2x - 1, 2y - 1, 2z - 1, 1), divided by w, so window depth 0.5 is clip depth 0; a scene with `orthogonalprojection` (the bit FUN_140186c90 sets at scene + 0x118 & 0x400) gets z = 0. The projection comes from the renderer's perspective builder (vtable slot +0x10 of the render device, 0x14009a360, called by the camera update with (fov, aspect, nearz, farz)); its disassembly is DirectXMath's right-handed perspective with the near and far arguments swapped (M22 = n / (f - n), M32 = n f / (f - n), M23 = -1), so depth is reversed, z_ndc = n (f - d) / (d (f - n)), 1 at the near plane and 0 at the far plane, and the pointer unprojects to the far plane exactly: the point on the cursor ray whose view-space depth is `farz`. The sibling FUN_14018e1a0 builds the hit-test ray from the same unprojection (origin the eye, direction toward the point). SceneRuntimeContext keeps the cursor in the canvas plane (m_cursor_plane_position, where the viewport maps the window; hit tests, the presented-content check and Scene::pointerScenePosition read it) and publishes to scripts a second value, ScriptCursorWorldPosition: for a display-sized scene (Scene::display_sized, the one with a perspective camera) with a perspective active camera, UnprojectNdcAtDepth (SceneCamera) places the cursor's NDC in the frame at `FarClip()` in front of the eye through the camera's inverse view and its fov and aspect; any other scene keeps the canvas point with z = 0. SetCursorWorldPosition, the probes' hook, sets both. Established: the decompiled functions above and the disassembly of the builder; Wallpaper Engine's own frame of workshop 3477054430 (a head script measuring the cursor from its layer's origin, neutral zone 100, 30 degrees of turn), captured with the cursor in the middle of the screen, shows the head at pitch -6.1 and yaw -61.4 degrees, and the far-plane point of the middle ray through that scene's camera gives -6.1 and -61.4 (canvas pixels gave about -15 and -6); workshop 3509243656 divides the value by 8000 and 9000 under a farz of 10000, where the far plane's half width at its fov and aspect is about 8300. Ours drawn end to end with the cursor in the middle (metal_scene_draw_smoke, LocalProjectsNamedByTheEnvironmentRunThroughTheNativeBackend with WE_TEST_INPUT_JSON) turns that head as Wallpaper Engine's frame does. Not established: a second capture with the cursor off the centre (the formula above fixes it, the unit test checks it through the projection), the shape of the cursor callbacks' event objects, whose position fields (and `input.cursorLocalPosition`) now carry the same point, and whether Wallpaper Engine's scripts run before or after it rewrites the view each frame (it unprojects when a script reads; here the point is fixed when the cursor is sampled, so a camera moved by a script or the shake in the same tick shows one frame later). Cost: one camera-view inverse and a few products per cursor sample, once a frame in a perspective scene (0.23 microseconds measured); nothing in a canvas scene. Tests: MouseInput.APerspectiveSceneHandsScriptsTheCursorRayPointAtTheFarPlane, .ThePerspectiveCursorPointLiesOnTheCursorRayOfAMovedAndShakenCamera (the point projects back to the pointer and lies farz deep for a turned, shaken camera), .ACameraPointAtDepthIsOnlyDefinedForAPerspectiveViewAndARealDepth, .AHeadScriptThatFollowsThePerspectiveCursorTurnsAsInWallpaperEngine (pitch -6.1, yaw -61.4), .ACanvasSceneKeepsTheCursorInCanvasUnitsEvenWithAPerspectiveCameraAround .APerspectiveSceneStillHitsLayersWhereTheyAreDrawn, .AParticleControlPointFollowsTheCanvasPlaneCursorInAPerspectiveScene (Scene::pointerScenePosition stays the canvas point) and .ThePerspectiveCursorPointFollowsThePictureWhenTheWindowCropsOrLetterboxesIt (the ray follows the cursor's place on the picture for a window that crops or letterboxes it).
sceneEngine.scriptedImageColorChanges: 2026-10-15: An image layer's colour that a script decides is the script's value every frame, as Wallpaper Engine draws it and as this renderer already drew a text layer's. ParseImageObj now resolves a `color` that carries a script, with or without a user binding, through ResolveVec3Setting (which builds the property script, init, update and media handlers included) and binds it with SceneRuntimeContext::BindMaterialColor to the layer's own material, every effect pass and a compose layer's passthrough, as a user-bound colour already was; until the script's first tick the layer holds the scene file's value. A colour script written as engine.on()/scene.on() handlers is queued as a scene script on its layer like the layer's visibility and origin scripts. Before, only a colour bound to a user property without a script was resolved, on the grounds that a binding would overwrite what a script that writes `thisLayer.color` and returns nothing just set (DynamicValue notifies on every update): so an exported update()/init()/mediaThumbnailChanged() colour script was never created for an image layer and the layer kept the scene file's colour for ever. That reason is met by the rule visibility and origin already follow: SceneRuntimeContext::SetNodeColor, the path of `thisLayer.color = ...`, also updates the value the layer's colour is bound to (BindMaterialColor now takes the layer's name and remembers the value, UnregisterNode forgets it), so a script that writes and returns nothing (PropertyScriptProgram::Evaluate hands back the current value for an undefined result) keeps what it wrote, the next update(value) is given it, and the write reaches every bound material instead of only the layer's own; a value update() returns, or a property change, still replaces it. Established against Wallpaper Engine 2.8.42's own frames: the media-widget template's colour script returns Vec3(0,0,0) until mediaThumbnailChanged brings a cover's colour, so the MP3 player display layer of 3151551777 (a solid layer authored 0.329 0.639 0.737) is black in Wallpaper Engine and was light teal here, and the cube and panel layers of 3819657300 (authored colours, the same script) are black-tinted in Wallpaper Engine where this renderer drew a red cube and a grey-tinted panel. Re-rendering both scenes with the change, against the pre-change binary of the same tree, turns the display black, and on the pixels the change moved in 3819657300 the mean absolute difference from Wallpaper Engine's frame falls from 47.9 to 17.9 (whole frame 9.46 to 9.35); neither scene's script errors changed. 12 of the 100 local scenes carry a scripted image colour, none of them on a layer that binds a cover (those drop their colour binding, unchanged). Semantics read from the scripts' own behaviour and the two scenes' frames, not from the binary (interoperability; no code copied). Not changed, and recorded in docs/testing/renderer.md: a text layer's colour is bound to a material constant applied every tick, so a script that only writes `thisLayer.color` on a text layer still loses the write (seen in a probe, not against a frame); a write to an image layer whose colour is bound to nothing still reaches only its own material. Cost: one script call per tick per scripted colour, as a text layer's colour script already pays, and an apply of three floats per bound material per tick; no pass, texture or allocation is added. The colour script is now a ScriptedDynamicValue, so DescribeTimeAdvancingWork reports SceneDemandReason::Script for it and a scene whose only script is an image layer's colour no longer idles (it did while no script was created); the 12 local scenes with a scripted image colour each carry 19 to 257 other scripts, so none of them changes. No wallpaper-specific rules. Tests: SceneSchema.ScriptedImageColourIsTheScriptsValueOnEveryLayerMaterial (a returned colour on a layer with an effect, nothing returned, a write over three ticks, a script whose next update(value) is given the colour it wrote, the media-widget template idle and after a cover, a colour script made of scene.on handlers, and the Script demand reason), SceneSchema.UserBoundImageColourTintsEveryLayerMaterialAndFollowsTheProperty (its scripted layer now follows its script, which was the old rule's assertion), MetalSceneDraw.AnImageLayersColourScriptDecidesItsColourOnBothRenderers (returned, write, nothing, plain, idle widget, cover, and a cover that arrives after frames were drawn, equal on both renderers), SceneSchema.AnImageLayersBrightnessTintsItsMaterialsOnlyInAnHdrSceneAndFollowsItsBindings (a returned and a written colour keep the layer's HDR brightness product, and stay the script's colour alone outside HDR); the script cases fail with the change removed.
sceneEngine.mdlTangentChanges: 2026-10-15: A model's signed tangent reaches the shader under the name Wallpaper Engine's model shaders declare. WE_IN_TANGENT (Scene/SpecTexs.hpp, written by WPMdlParser::GenMeshFromMdl for a model that carries tangents) is `a_Tangent4`, where it was `a_Tangent`; generic, generic2, generic3, generic4, genericimage3, genericimage4, chroma4, foliage4 and fur4 declare `attribute vec4 a_Tangent4` under NORMALMAP (the two genericimage shaders for a lit, skinned puppet layer). Why: both renderers bind a vertex input to the mesh attribute of the same name and give an input the mesh lacks the first vertex buffer at offset 0, so under the old name a lit, normal-mapped model's tangent was the first four floats of its vertex (position.xyz and, in a model without bones, normal.x); the bitangent cross(N,T)*w and the perturbed normal (generic4.frag takes it as T*n.x + B*n.y + N*n.z and passes it to PerformLighting_V1 without normalising) were then far from unit length, and the highlight swept through the specular pole: hard-edged patches, contour lines and white 3x3 sparkles on a lit roof. How established: the declaration name and the fragment stage from Wallpaper Engine 2.8.42's own shaders (shaders/generic4.vert, generic4.frag, common_vertex.h, genericimage4.vert, base/model_vertex_v1.h) and the lack of any other name for it in any of them (no shader there declares `a_Tangent`); WE's frame of the affected scene (a smooth specular pool and a soft streak on the roof, no sparkles); a temporary trace in both renderers' vertex binders over the 101 local scene projects, which printed `a_Tangent4` unbound on `generic4` for exactly one scene before the change and for none after (the only other input a mesh lacked was `flat`'s `a_Color`, 41 scenes: flat.vert declares it unconditionally and reads it only under VERTEXCOLOR); and a before/after render of that scene with the native renderer at 1728x964 after 8 s, whose roof had 27 pixels at 235 or above on all channels and 36 at 200 or above before and none after, the compatibility renderer drawing the same picture as the native one in both runs. Nothing else read the name (no other consumer in the engine, the shader crate or the app), no pass, buffer or per-frame work is added, and a model without a normal map never read the attribute. Left alone: the offset-0 fallback for an input a mesh lacks (logging it or binding zeros would flag `flat`'s unused `a_Color` in 41 scenes and needs use information reflection does not carry; see Known limitations in docs/testing/renderer.md). Tests: mdl_schema_tests MdlSchema.VersionedSurfaceMeshesPreserveAllVertexAttributes and .GenMeshIncludesNormals now expect `a_Tangent4` (they encoded the old name), and metal_scene_draw_smoke MetalSceneDraw.AModelsTangentReachesTheShaderThatDeclaresItOnBothRenderers draws a model-parser quad with a tangent that is no axis and handedness -1 through a probe shader that builds the tangent and bitangent as generic4 does (BuildTangentSpace without the model transform; Wallpaper Engine's shaders are not in the repository), showing the tangent, the bitangent and a perturbed normal as flat colours that must equal the mesh's own values on both renderers; all fail without the change.
sceneEngine.imageBrightnessChanges: 2026-10-15: An image layer's brightness reaches the shader as Wallpaper Engine's layer draw hands it over, for interoperability; no code copied. The layer draw (FUN_140208670) and the effect layer's final composite (FUN_140207740) both write the draw colour as (colour x (ctx+0x118 & 0x2000 ? brightness : 1), alpha), the flag being the one that picks the 16F back buffer and so the HDR pipeline (scene.hdr here: hdr with bloom on), and the effect chain's own passes are drawn with white; the layer object's brightness field (+0x340) is read by these two draws and by no other layer-draw function found, so a shader's g_Brightness is its material constant. ParseImageObj exported brightness only as the uniform g_Brightness, which the shaders that take the tint through g_Color4 (genericimage3, genericimage4, genericimage2 with VERSION) do not declare, so they lost it, and a user-bound or scripted image brightness had no live binding. g_Color4 now carries colour x brightness in an HDR scene and the colour alone elsewhere, on the layer's material, each effect pass and the compose passthrough; SceneMaterial::tint keeps colour and brightness apart so BindMaterialColor, SetNodeColor and the new BindMaterialBrightness (a user property or a property script, as the text path binds it) rebuild the product from both; the layer's brightness is no longer also g_Brightness: the shaders that declare one declare it as a material property (ui_editor_properties_hdr_brightness / Brightness) and multiply their albedo by it under #if HDR (the stock generic2, generic3, generic4, chroma4, foliage4 and fur4; WPSceneParser sets that combo to scene.hdr) or unconditionally (genericimage, and genericimage2 without VERSION, which declares it instead of g_Color4), and the decompile reads the layer's brightness for the draw colour only, so the layer's value is not also given to a material's own g_Brightness (no stock shader declares both g_Brightness and g_Color4). Established: the decompile above, and Wallpaper Engine's frame of a scene with a girl layer at brightness 0.9 (user property glow) under a colour-burn gradient: the left background fits 2.3 levels once the layer is x0.9 (29 without it), the jacket 3.7 (16 without), and the fit is sharp at 0.9. Cost: one multiply of three constants when a layer is built or its colour or brightness changes; nothing per frame. Tests: SceneSchema.AnImageLayersBrightnessTintsItsMaterialsOnlyInAnHdrSceneAndFollowsItsBindings; MetalSceneDraw.AnImageLayersBrightnessTintsItOnlyWhereTheSceneRendersHdrOnBothRenderers and .AnImageLayersBoundBrightnessFollowsItsPropertyAndScriptOnBothRenderers (both renderers, with and without an effect and a g_Brightness shader, HDR, HDR without bloom and SDR).
sceneEngine.composeParallaxChanges: 2026-10-15: A compose layer drawn through effects holds the screen behind the place camera parallax draws its card, for interoperability; no code copied. Wallpaper Engine's per-frame draw loop (FUN_14018aac0, 284547-284605, entered with the scene's orthographic and parallax bits set) adds one offset, (the outermost parent's origin - the eased cursor point, a scene-level value that includes the shaken eye) * cameraparallaxamount * the root's parallaxDepth, to the translation of the object's model matrix on its matrix stack and then draws the object, so every pass of the layer reads that matrix: the composelayer pass, which maps its card onto the screen (composelayer.vert: v_ScreenCoord = the card position through g_ModelViewProjectionMatrix, xyw), reads the screen where the layer's last pass draws the card. Ours gave a layer drawn through effects a zero depth on its own node (the depth is on its effect passes), and a compose layer without children frames its effects, and so draws its first pass, with a camera at the origin rather than the scene camera (a layer with children has its first pass drawn through the scene camera, which the render graph names), so WPShaderValueUpdater::UpdateUniforms moved the last pass only: the first pass read the screen at the unshifted place and the card showed the scene displaced by its own parallax offset, a hard-edged slab wherever the effect keeps the copy (an audio-bar layer whose visualizer draws nothing in silence). UpdateUniforms now takes the depth of a pass that reads the screen (the composelayer material) from NodeParallaxDepth, which asks the layer's effect passes first, and measures the offset from the scene camera the pass's matrix is built with instead of the camera that draws the pass (the two differ for a layer without children only); FrameVaryingUniforms reports kParallax for that pass by the same rule. An ordinary effect layer's first pass, which draws into the layer's own target, is still not moved, nor is a compose layer drawn into a composite through a layer-local camera. A depth a script writes (SetNodeParallaxDepth) used to be written into the record of the layer's own node as well as its effect passes, when it had one (the parser gives every layer drawn through effects one, at zero): an ordinary effect layer's first pass was then moved inside its own target, and a layer that already followed the cursor reported a change, which asks for a new render graph. A layer drawn through effects now takes a written depth on its effect passes alone. Established: the decompiled loop; the comparison of Wallpaper Engine's frames with ours for a scene whose sword audio-bar compose layers (depth 2.8 and 3.2 under one group, copy-only transparency) drew a rectangle of displaced scene about 1790 by 340 px over the sword in ours and a continuous picture in Wallpaper Engine; a block match placed our slab at the displacement the missing offset predicts, and with cameraparallax off it vanished. Not established: a local corpus has 15 compose layers with effects at a non-zero depth in 7 scenes with camera parallax on, none of them with children or nested in another compose layer, and only the scene above was compared with Wallpaper Engine's frames; the other six change too, with no recorded before and after check. A compose layer with effects nested in another compose layer is not exercised (its last pass is drawn through the parent's camera and its first through the scene camera; whether Wallpaper Engine's offsets differ there was not examined). Cost: one map lookup per compose first pass per frame, no added pass; that pass is now reported as following the cursor like the layer's last pass, so its target is not reused while a scene with camera parallax runs. Tests: ScriptRuntimeCompat.AComposeLayersFirstPassReadsTheScreenWhereParallaxDrawsItsCard (the first pass's model-view-projection equals its card's for a layer with children, drawn through the scene camera as the render graph names it, and one without, with the cursor centred and away from it, and again after a script writes a depth; unmoved in a layer-local composite and for an ordinary effect layer, written depth included; with its kParallax report) and MetalSceneDraw.AComposeLayerHoldsWhatIsBehindWhereParallaxDrawsItOnBothRenderers (a compose layer, alone and over a child, through an effect that inverts red, in a depth-2 group over an asymmetric backdrop, equals the backdrop with red inverted where the layer is drawn and changes nothing outside it, on both renderers); both fail without the change, and with the depth half alone the layer without children still fails.
sceneEngine.textureMipBudgetChanges: 2026-10-15: A packaged texture keeps its full-size mip level unless the next level still covers the display, as Wallpaper Engine draws it from the full-size level, for interoperability; no code copied. Established by comparing Wallpaper Engine 2.8.42's own frame of a scene whose only image layer is a 4240x2369 JPEG-container texture (TEXB0003, five levels) on a 3456x2024 surface with ours: ours drew level 1 (2120x1184) magnified about 1.8 times. Fitting the texture-to-screen mapping on both frames (normalised cross-correlation 0.995 on ours), the Laplacian energy of Wallpaper Engine's frame matched a level 0 rendering of the decoded texture (about 89% of it, the ratio ours shows against level 1) and was twice a level 1 rendering; the layer has no effects, bloom or HDR. The texture-surface budget of 78ebc9c6 (textureResidencyChanges) rounded the surface's longest edge up to a power of two and dropped every leading level longer than that ceiling, so a texture between the ceiling and about twice the screen footprint (4240 px on a 3456 px surface, 2560 px on 1920x1080) lost its full-size level and was magnified by up to 2x. IImageParser::SetTextureSurfaceSize now keeps the surface's longest side, and WPTexImageParser::Parse drops a leading level only while the next level's header (read ahead without moving the stream or decoding) is at least that long; the kept level covers the surface unless the texture is smaller, and a chain whose levels already fit selects what it did (powers of two included). Sprite, video, multi-slot and unknown-container exclusions, layout metadata, render targets, frame time and per-frame work are unchanged. Cost, decided by the owner: texture memory grows only for textures in that band. Modelled from the unpacked mip headers of the local library's 143 layer textures, as sums over the whole library (the largest single scene is about 99 MB at 1920x1080 and about 103 MB at 2560x1440 and 3456x2024), +243 MB at 1920x1080 (16 textures in 8 scenes), +141 MB at 2560x1440 (3 in 2) and +184 MB at 3456x2024 (4 in 3); the 4240x2369 texture goes from about 13 MB to 51 MB. Not measured in a running app. Not done: choosing each layer's level from its projected extent, which would also fix layers drawn larger than the display and, modelled the same way, would cost about 110 MB more than the display rule at 2560x1440 summed over the library (docs/testing/renderer.md, Known limitations). Tests: TexSchema.SurfaceBudgetKeepsALevelThatTheNextOneWouldNotCover, .SurfaceBudgetKeepsTheSmallestLevelThatStillCoversTheSurface and .SurfaceBudgetFollowsTheHeaderSizesOfAnEncodedChain (fail without the change; the three existing SurfaceBudget tests pass both ways), MetalSceneDraw.ATextureWhoseNextLevelFallsShortOfTheSurfaceKeepsItsFullSizeLevelOnBothRenderers (a 528x352 chain, white first level and black others, drawn across a 384x256 surface: the first level blended with the second on both renderers, black without the change).
sceneEngine.textParallaxChanges: 2026-10-15: A text layer drawn straight onto the scene is moved by camera parallax like any other layer, for interoperability; no code copied. Wallpaper Engine's per-frame draw loop (FUN_14018aac0, entered with the scene's orthographic and parallax bits both set) visits every object of the scene's draw list whatever its kind, climbs to the outermost parent and adds (that root's origin - the eased cursor point) * cameraparallaxamount * the root's parallaxDepth to the object's model matrix; text objects are drawn by that loop and the editor serialises parallaxDepth on them. ParseTextObj made no WPShaderValueData for a text layer without effects, so WPShaderValueUpdater::UpdateUniforms found no node data and never added the offset: the layer stood still when the cursor moved and sat (origin - centre) * amount * depth off the place its neighbours reach at rest, while image, shape, particle and effect layers of the same depth moved. It now registers the record an image layer without effects has (SetNodeData on the card node with the object's parallaxDepth), so the offset, the layer-tree anchoring of ResolveLayerParallax, a script's parallaxDepth write and the kParallax report that keeps its target out of static reuse all apply; a text drawn through effects keeps its depth on its effect passes and gets no second record, so it is moved once. Established: the decompiled loop, and Wallpaper Engine's frame of a scene (cameraparallax on, amount 0.15) whose date label, depth 0.06, sat 8 px above ours and 5 units right of it beside an underline of the same depth that already matched; with the fix ours lands within a pixel of it in both directions, and no layer that was not text changes. Cost: none beyond an image layer's: one model-matrix update for the text pass; a scene with camera parallax on no longer reuses a target that only a text layer of non-zero depth draws into, as for any parallax layer. Tests: TextObjectRuntime.CameraParallaxMovesAPlainTextLayerByItsDepth and .ATextLayerUnderAGroupRidesTheGroupsParallax; MetalSceneDraw.CameraParallaxMovesATextLayerAsItMovesAnImageOnBothRenderers (the text and a square of the same depth move alike on both renderers, with the cursor centred and away from the centre, and a text through a copy effect is moved once).
sceneEngine.mediaIdleStateChanges: 2026-10-15: A scene is told it has no player. SceneRuntimeContext::Tick calls DispatchIdleMediaState once, on the first tick after the scene scripts' own tick (so every script has started) and before the camera and the draw: every script gets `mediaPropertiesChanged` with an empty track (the object the app sends with integration on and nothing playing) and `mediaPlaybackChanged` with `PLAYBACK_STOPPED`, whether or not the user turned media integration on, and without waiting for that consent because it names no one's music; what a player really reports is still dropped while the setting is off (DispatchMediaEventJson is unchanged). A real event of either type that reached the scene before that tick (the replay of the current state to a scene that has just attached) is not repeated as idle, per type (NoteMediaEventTold reads only the `type` of the JSON until the idle state is decided), and a real event afterwards is delivered as usual. Wallpaper Engine's media widgets are authored visible and hide themselves on PLAYBACK_STOPPED, so a scene that was never told (integration off, which is the app's default, or no player) drew every group, cover and mascot of them. Established against Wallpaper Engine 2.8.42's own frames of a scene with such a widget (3819684521): with nothing playing, the 'Media Area' group, whose visible script is `thisLayer.visible = event.state !== MediaPlaybackEvent.PLAYBACK_STOPPED`, and the dancing puppet parented to it are absent in both shots, where this renderer drew the puppet over the blue tang; the same scene rendered with one synthetic STOPPED event drew none either, and with this change it draws none with no event at all. Wallpaper Engine's media integration defaults to on (the missing `mediaintegration` key is set to true, FUN_140046f20, and handed to the media manager), for interoperability; no code copied. The event dispatch itself was not located in the binary, and a start-paused scale timeline on that group (not followed here, see the known limitations) could also hide it there, so the order of init and the first event and the absence of a timeline or thumbnail event at idle rest on the frames and on what the app's own relay sends a web page with no player. Cost: one dispatch of two small events to each script at load; nothing per frame. Tests: SceneScriptMediaEventSmoke.ASceneNoPlayerFeedsIsToldNothingIsPlayingOnItsFirstTick, .ARealStateTheSceneHeardBeforeItsFirstTickIsNotRepeatedAsIdle, .TheIdleStateFillsInOnlyWhatNoRealEventSaid, .ARealEventAfterTheIdleStateIsDeliveredLikeAnyOther; MetalSceneDraw.AMediaWidgetIsHiddenWhileNothingPlaysOnBothRenderers, .AMediaWidgetShowsWhileSomethingPlaysOnBothRenderers, .ANoMusicPlaceholderShowsWhileNothingPlaysOnBothRenderers.
sceneEngine.coverSlotChanges: 2026-10-15: A texture slot bound to the now-playing cover (a `usertextures` entry of type `system`, `$mediaThumbnail` or `$mediaPreviousThumbnail`, in an image layer's material or one of its effect passes) keeps the picture its author left in that slot until the runtime has a cover to put there, as Wallpaper Engine draws it. ApplySystemUserTextures, given the scene's RuntimeImageSource, binds such a slot through the new RuntimeImageSource::BindCoverSlot, which returns a runtime image name (`<cover>|<authored texture>`) that Parse() resolves to the track's cover while one is published and to the authored picture while it is not (before the first track and again after the explicit clear); Version() follows the cover's own version, so both renderers swap it on the version check they already make every frame, with no graph rebuild and no extra pass. The authored picture is decoded on first use (after the texture budget is set), kept resident, and never substituted when the slot has no texture, or holds a video, a sprite sheet, a render target or another layer's composite, or a one- or two-channel picture (a mask or normal map reads through other channels than a cover's). The native renderer's runtime image ring now uploads block-compressed pictures and every mip level the image holds, and its sampler follows the image the name shows now, as the compatibility backend's does, so a cover stays clamped whatever the art's flags say. The layer colour is still forced to white for a layer that binds a cover; whether Wallpaper Engine tints the idle art with it is not established. Established against Wallpaper Engine 2.8.42: its own frames of a cover layer with nothing playing show the authored texture at the cover's position, not a blank slot (3819637149: the instance's `wayside` art inside the rim, where this renderer drew only the rim), and the 2.8.42 binary delivers the cover as a user property written only when a thumbnail event arrives (FUN_140171440 stores `$mediaThumbnail` as `mediaThumbnail_<n>.system` on a thumbnail change and `$mediaPreviousThumbnail` only when a previous one exists; FUN_140154480 reads a pass's `usertextures` types `system` and `usershortcut`), the way an unset `scenetexture` property already leaves the authored texture (interoperability; no code copied). After the change a layer whose own picture sits in a cover slot draws it while idle, closer to Wallpaper Engine's frame (3465215190, blurred error 8.95 to 7.89). Cost: one decoded authored picture stays resident per distinct cover name and authored texture (0.35 MB for a 512x512 DXT5 with mips; 2.9 MB for the largest local, 736x736 RGBA8), and the native renderer's two in-flight ring textures hold it while it shows; nothing is added per frame (an idle slot is the integer version check) and a cover change is at most one upload per frame in flight. Tests: MetalSceneDraw.ACoverSlotShowsItsAuthoredTextureUntilACoverArrivesOnBothRenderers, MetalSceneDraw.ACoverIsSampledClampedWhateverItsAuthoredPictureAskedForOnBothRenderers, MetalSceneDraw.AnIdleCoverSlotUploadsItsPictureOnceAndACoverChangeCostsOneUploadPerFrameInFlight, CoverSlot.* in media_thumbnail_texture_smoke.
sceneEngine.wallpaperFramingChanges: 2026-10-13: The presented wallpaper can sit anywhere in the room the display leaves around it, not only in the middle. A new header-only Presentation/WallpaperFraming.hpp, free of Vulkan includes so that SceneWallpaper.hpp can use it and included by WallpaperScaling.hpp, holds WallpaperFraming (pan_x, pan_y: fractions of the slack, 0 the left or top edge, 1 the right or bottom edge, 0.5 the centre) and NormalizeWallpaperFraming (clamped to [0, 1], a non-finite axis becomes the centre); ComputeWallpaperScalingLayout (WallpaperScaling.cpp) takes the two fractions as trailing parameters defaulting to 0.5 and replaces its two `* 0.5` factors with them, so the slack, negative when Fill or a scale above 1 overflows the display and positive when Fit, Original size or a scale below 1 leaves bars, is split by one formula and the default is bit-exact with the previous layout. The scissor, ComputeWallpaperCursorMapping and MakeWallpaperViewport are untouched: the pointer mapping derives from the viewport rectangle, so hit testing follows the position. SceneWallpaper gains PROPERTY_FRAMING and setFraming (one object message, so the axes never tear), RenderHandler::CMD_SET_FRAMING (in the CASE_CMD list) stores m_framing beside the scaling factor and re-applies it in reapplySurfaceState and rebuildRenderGraph, SceneRendererHandle forwards SetWallpaperFraming, and both MetalRender and VulkanRender hold the value, pass it to their scaling layout and invalidate the present gate (the present key already holds the viewport rectangle). The C ABI gains owe_scene_wallpaper_set_framing(scene, pan_x, pan_y), live, retained before the first frame, null scene or non-finite value an error through owe_last_error, no logging on the path; bindgen picks it up through the owe_ allowlist. The Rust engine calls it (OweScene::set_framing, from open_scene and from SceneRuntime) and so does the sandboxed lock-screen extension directly (Extension/WallpaperSurface.swift); the app's Position sliders reach it through the bridge.
